items.claim: Theorem: The measure of the inscribed angle is half the measure of the central angle, subtended by the same arc.

items.text: Given: $\angle ACB$ is an inscribed angle, $\angle AMB$ is a central angle.

items.quote: Prove that m (∠ ACB) = 1/2 m (∠ AMB).
items.text: R.T.P.: Prove that $m(\angle ACB) = \frac{1}{2} m(\angle AMB)$.

items.quote: There are three cases to prove this theorem.
items.text: Proof: There are three cases to prove this theorem.

items.quote: If M belongs to one of the two sides of the inscribed angle.
items.caption: Case 1: circle with centre M on side CA... M lies on chord CB; points C (top), A (right), B (bottom); segments CA, MA, with C, M, B collinear.

items.quote: If M is a point inside the inscribed angle.

items.quote: If M is a point outside the inscribed angle.
items.caption: Case 3: circle with M outside the inscribed angle; points C (top right), A (right), B (bottom), M (left of angle); dashed line through C, M extended; segments MA, MB, CA, CB.

items.quote: First case: If M belongs to one of the two sides
items.text: First case: If M belongs to one of the two sides of the inscribed angle.

items.quote: ∠AMB is outside Δ AMC
items.text: Since $\angle AMB$ is outside $\Delta AMC$; therefore $m(\angle AMB) = m(\angle A) + m(\angle C)$ (1). Since $AM = CM$ (radii lengths), therefore $m(\angle A) = m(\angle C)$ (2). From (1) and (2) we get: $m(\angle AMB = 2\, m(\angle C)$; therefore $m(\angle ACB) = \frac{1}{2} m(\angle AMB)$ (Q.E.D)

items.quote: Prove that the theorem in the other two cases are correct
items.text: Prove that the theorem in the other two cases are correct and save your work in the portfolio.

items.stem: A is a point outside the circle M, $\overrightarrow{AB}$ is a tangent to the circle at B, $\overrightarrow{AM}$ intersects the circle M at C and D respectively, $m(\angle A)=40^\circ$. Find with proof $m(\angle BDC)$.
solution: Given: $\overrightarrow{AB}$ is a tangent to the circle at B, $m(\angle A)=40^\circ$, $\overrightarrow{AM}$ intersects the circle M at C and D.
Proof: ∵ $\overrightarrow{AB}$ is tangent to the circle at B, $\overline{BM}$ is a radius.
∵ Inscribed $\angle BDC$ and central $\angle BMC$ are both subtended at $\widehat{BC}$.

items.text: In the opposite figure: $\overline{AB}$ is a chord of circle M, $\overline{MC}\perp\overline{AB}$. Prove that: $m(\angle AMC)=m(\angle ADB)$. items.quote: Well known problem (1)
items.stem: Well known problem (1): If two chords intersect at a point inside a circle, then the measure of the included angle equals half of the sum of the measure of the two opposite arcs.
solution: R.T.P.: m(∠AEC) = ½ [m(arc AC) + m(arc BD)]
∵ m(∠AEC) = m(∠D) + m(∠A) = ½ m(arc AC) + ½ m(arc BD)
items.notes: Given line printed with overbars on AB and CD (chords) rather than segments.

items.quote: D A E C B
items.caption: Circle with chords AB and CD... chords through D–E–... and B–E–A... intersecting at E; dashed segment AD; angle at E marked; points D, A, E, C, B.

items.quote: Well known problem (2)
items.stem: Well known problem (2): If two rays carrying two chords in a circle are intersecting outside it, then the measure of their intersecting angle equals half of the measure of the major arc subtracted from it half of the measure of the minor arc in which both are included by the two sides of this angle.
solution: Proof: ∵ $\angle ABC$ is exterior to $\triangle BEC$.
items.notes: Solution has no separate final answer; ends with Q.E.D.

learning_objectives.label: Inscribed and central angle relation
learning_objectives.description: Calculate the measure of an inscribed angle or of the central angle subtended by the same arc, using the theorem that the inscribed angle is half the central angle.

learning_objectives.label: Inscribed angle and arc measure
learning_objectives.description: Calculate an inscribed angle from its subtended arc, find arc measures from angles, and show that an angle in a semicircle is a right angle.

learning_objectives.label: Angles from intersecting chords and rays
learning_objectives.description: Calculate the angle formed by two chords intersecting inside a circle, or by two rays intersecting outside it, using half the sum or half the difference of the intercepted arcs.
